title: My World
subtitle: All About Me

project.title: My World Profile
project.description: Create a personal profile and introduce the people who are important to you. The project grows lesson by lesson.
project.deliverable: A personal profile with an identity card and a family tree, presented in simple English.
successCriteria: I can introduce myself and give basic personal information.
I can name countries and nationalities.
I can use be in affirmative, negative and question forms.
I can talk about family members and relationships.
I can use plural nouns, possessive adjectives and demonstratives.
I can present my family tree in simple English.
I can use have got in affirmative, negative and question forms.
I can use object pronouns and the articles a, an and the.

objectives: Introduce yourself and ask for basic personal information.
Name family members and describe family relationships.
Use regular and irregular plural nouns.
Use possessive adjectives and this, that, these and those.
Create and present a personal profile and family tree.
Use have got, object pronouns and articles a / an / the.

vocabulary.example: How do you spell your name?

grammar.title: Verb be
grammar.rule: I am / I'm · He/She/It is / He's/She's/It's · You/We/They are / You're/We're/They're. Negative: I'm not · isn't · aren't. Questions: Am I? Is he/she/it? Are you/we/they?
examples: They aren't in the same class.
Are you from England? No, I'm not.

grammar.title: Possessive adjectives
grammar.rule: I → my · you → your · he → his · she → her · it → its · we → our · they → their

grammar.title: Demonstratives
grammar.rule: Near: this (singular), these (plural). Far: that (singular), those (plural).

screens.title: First meeting · Marie and Mateo
screens.body: Listen to the original dialogue. Then work in pairs and practise reading it.
screens.audioText: Marie: Hello. I'm Marie. What's your name? Mateo: My name's Mateo. Marie: It's nice to meet you, Mateo. How do you spell your name? Mateo: M-A-T-E-O. Marie: How old are you? Mateo: I'm 16. And you? Marie: I'm 15. Are you from England? Mateo: No, I'm not. I'm Italian. Marie: Are you from Rome? Is it nice? Mateo: Yes, it's very nice.

questions.q: How do you spell his name?

Child has an irregular plural: children.
The plural used here is people.
A consonant + y changes to -ies.
A consonant + y changes to -ies.

screens.title: Grammar Insight · have got
screens.rule: Affirmative: I / we / you / they have got (’ve got); he / she / it has got (’s got). Negative: haven’t got / hasn’t got. Questions: Have + I / we / you / they + got …? Has + he / she / it + got …? Short answers: Yes, I have. / No, we haven’t. Yes, he has. / No, she hasn’t.
examples: He has got short hair and blue eyes.
Have you got a computer? — Yes, I have.

questions.why: With we, use haven’t got.
Parents is plural, so use haven’t got.
With he, she and it, use has got in affirmative forms and Has … got? in questions.

questions.q: A: Has Anna got a new bag? B: No, she ___.
questions.why: The short negative answer is No, she hasn’t.
With I, use have got.
With a singular subject, use has got.
With Tom (he), use hasn’t got.

screens.title: Match the sentence halves · have got
screens.text: Match each beginning with the correct ending. This activity is based on Grammar Reference W.4, Exercise 2.

options: c. big house, but it’s nice.
b. a brother and a cat.
items.answer: b. a brother and a cat.

screens.title: Grammar Insight · object pronouns
screens.rule: Subject pronouns name the person or thing doing the action. Object pronouns receive the action or follow a preposition.
examples: I like the boy. → I like him.
Jude likes me and my friends.
We are with the girl. → We are with her.

questions.q: I like the boy. I like ___.
questions.why: Him is the object pronoun for he.

questions.q: Jude likes me and my friends. Jude likes ___.
questions.why: Us is the object pronoun for we.

questions.q: We are with the girl. We are with ___.
questions.why: Her is the object pronoun for she.

questions.q: I haven’t got your books. I haven’t got ___.
questions.why: Them is the object pronoun for they.

questions.q: She’s got my bag. She’s got ___.
questions.why: It is the object pronoun for a singular thing.

screens.title: Grammar Insight · articles a, an and the
screens.rule: Use a before a singular noun beginning with a consonant sound. Use an before a singular noun beginning with a vowel sound. Use a / an when mentioning something for the first time, describing a person or thing, or saying someone's job. Use the before singular or plural nouns when something has already been mentioned or there is only one of it in the context.
examples: a ball · a desk · a tree
There is a house near my school.
I’ve got a new computer and a new phone. I like the computer but I don’t like the phone.

questions.q: They’ve got ___ new house and a new car.
questions.why: New begins with a consonant sound, so use a.

questions.q: They’ve got a new house and a new car. ___ car is red.
questions.why: The refers to the car already mentioned.
The is used for a place understood as the one relevant in this context.
Brother begins with a consonant sound.

questions.q: There’s ___ computer club and ___ music club at our school.
questions.why: Both computer and music begin with consonant sounds.
The club has already been mentioned.

questions.q: He’s ___ old man and he’s got ___ big dog.
questions.why: Old begins with a vowel sound; big begins with a consonant sound.
Maths begins with a consonant sound.
